title: Climate Change Sparks New, Faster-Moving Landslides: Gizmodo Uncovers the Emerging Threat
body:
A massive, house‑sized slab of permafrost ripped from a hillside and surged down a remote valley in Canada’s Northwest Territories last year, exposing a new class of landslide that scientists say is being amplified by a warming climate. The 2017 event, which carved a two‑mile scar through the Johnson River Valley, is the first documented instance of “permafrost flow” – a phenomenon where frozen ground thaws, loses cohesion and behaves like a slow‑moving glacier of ice and soil. Researchers now warn that such slides could become far more common across the Arctic as rising temperatures destabilize the continent’s once‑solid frozen crust.

The Johnson River incident began when a section of permafrost, estimated to be roughly the size of a modest home, detached from a steep slope and accelerated down the valley at speeds of up to 15 metres per second. The slide left a deep gouge in the terrain, exposing layers of ancient sediment and disrupting the river’s flow. While landslides are not unusual in mountainous regions, the mechanics of this event differ markedly from the rock‑and‑soil failures familiar to geologists. In a permafrost flow, the frozen matrix thaws from the inside out, creating a lubricated, semi‑liquid mixture that can travel great distances before finally settling.

Climate scientists have long predicted that a warming Arctic would destabilize permafrost, releasing greenhouse gases and threatening infrastructure. The Johnson River slide provides a tangible, visual confirmation that the thaw is not merely a slow, invisible process but can trigger sudden, dramatic geomorphic change. “We are witnessing a transition from a static frozen landscape to a dynamic, fluid one,” says Dr. Elena Martinez, a cryosphere specialist at the University of Alberta. “The energy balance shift caused by even a few degrees of warming is enough to melt the ice that cements the soil, turning a solid slab into a viscous flow.”

The implications extend beyond academic curiosity. Indigenous communities across northern Canada already report increasing difficulty in maintaining traditional travel routes and hunting grounds as the ground becomes uneven and unpredictable. Infrastructure built on permafrost—roads, pipelines, and buildings—faces heightened risk of subsidence and collapse. In the Johnson River region, the slide blocked a seasonal access road, forcing emergency repairs and prompting a reevaluation of land‑use planning in the area. Moreover, the exposed sediment may release trapped carbon and methane, feeding back into the global climate system.

Internationally, the phenomenon adds urgency to monitoring programs that have traditionally focused on coastal erosion and sea‑level rise. Satellite imagery, ground‑penetrating radar, and drone surveys are now being deployed to map permafrost stability across the circumpolar north. Researchers are developing predictive models that integrate temperature projections, soil composition, and topography to identify hotspots where permafrost flows could emerge. Early warning systems could give communities critical lead time to adapt or relocate vulnerable assets.

As the Arctic continues to warm at twice the rate of the global average, the Johnson River landslide may become a harbinger of a new era of geohazards. Policymakers, engineers, and scientists must collaborate to incorporate permafrost dynamics into risk assessments, infrastructure design, and climate‑adaptation strategies. The slide serves as a stark reminder that climate change is reshaping the planet’s physical foundations, turning once‑stable frozen ground into a moving, unpredictable force. Anticipating and mitigating these emerging threats will be essential to safeguarding northern ecosystems and the people who depend on them.
